title: Carnot Cycle and Carnot Theorem
short_intro: The Carnot cycle is an idealized reversible thermodynamic cycle composed of two isothermal and two adiabatic processes operating between two thermal reservoirs. It establishes the theoretical upper limit for the efficiency of any heat engine operating between the same two temperatures.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Understanding the four stages of the Carnot cycle on a P-V diagram, efficiency formula in terms of absolute temperatures (1 - T₂/T₁), and working of a Carnot heat engine and refrigerator.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Derivation of work done, efficiency of Carnot engine with an ideal gas working substance, Carnot's theorem, thermodynamic temperature scale, and coefficient of performance for refrigerators and heat pumps.

prerequisites: Concept of Temperature and Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics
First and Second Laws of Thermodynamics
Equation of state for ideal gases (PV = nRT) and adiabatic processes (PV^γ = constant)

concept_notes.heading: Stages of the Carnot Cycle
bullets: Stage 1: Isothermal expansion at source temperature T₁ where the working substance absorbs heat Q₁ from the reservoir at constant temperature.
Stage 2: Adiabatic expansion where the system expands without heat exchange, causing the temperature to drop from T₁ to sink temperature T₂.
Stage 3: Isothermal compression at sink temperature T₂ where heat Q₂ is rejected to the cold reservoir.
Stage 4: Adiabatic compression back to the initial state, raising the temperature from T₂ to T₁.

concept_notes.heading: Efficiency of a Carnot Engine
bullets: Thermal efficiency η is defined as the ratio of net work done (W) to the heat absorbed from the hot reservoir (Q₁).
For a complete cycle, η = W / Q₁ = (Q₁ - Q₂) / Q₁ = 1 - (Q₂ / Q₁).
Since heat transfer in isothermal processes is proportional to absolute temperatures, Q₂ / Q₁ = T₂ / T₁, yielding η = 1 - (T₂ / T₁).

concept_notes.heading: Carnot's Theorem
bullets: Statement 1: No heat engine operating between two given thermal reservoirs can be more efficient than a reversible Carnot engine operating between the same two reservoirs.
Statement 2: All reversible heat engines operating between the same two thermal reservoirs have the same efficiency, regardless of the working substance.
The efficiency depends solely on the temperatures of the source and the sink: η_max = 1 - (T₂ / T₁).

concept_notes.heading: Thermodynamic Temperature Scale
bullets: Kelvin temperature scale is independent of the physical properties of any particular working substance.
The ratio of heats absorbed and rejected by a Carnot engine is equal to the ratio of absolute temperatures of the reservoirs: Q₁ / Q₂ = T₁ / T₂.
Absolute zero (0 K) is the temperature at which the efficiency of a Carnot engine becomes 100%, which is unattainable in practice.

derivations.title: Efficiency of Carnot Engine using an Ideal Gas
derivations.conditions: One mole of an ideal gas as the working substance undergoing a quasi-static Carnot cycle.
steps: Step 1: For Isothermal Expansion (1 to 2 at T₁), work done W₁₂ = RT₁ ln(V₂ / V₁). Heat absorbed Q₁ = W₁₂.
Step 2: For Adiabatic Expansion (2 to 3), T₁V₂^(γ-1) = T₂V₃^(γ-1). Work done W₂₃ = R(T₁ - T₂)/(γ - 1).
Step 3: For Isothermal Compression (3 to 4 at T₂), work done W₃₄ = RT₂ ln(V₄ / V₃) = -RT₂ ln(V₃ / V₄). Heat rejected Q₂ = -W₃₄.
Step 4: For Adiabatic Compression (4 to 1), T₂V₄^(γ-1) = T₁V₁^(γ-1). Using V₂/V₁ = V₃/V₄ from adiabatic relations, net work W = Q₁ - Q₂ = RT₁ ln(V₂/V₁) - RT₂ ln(V₂/V₁).
Step 5: Efficiency η = W / Q₁ = (RT₁ - RT₂) ln(V₂/V₁) / (RT₁ ln(V₂/V₁)) = 1 - (T₂ / T₁).

derivations.title: Coefficient of Performance (COP) of Carnot Refrigerator
derivations.conditions: Reversed Carnot cycle operating between temperatures T₂ (cold sink) and T₁ (hot source).
steps: Step 1: A refrigerator extracts heat Q₂ from the cold reservoir by consuming external work W.
Step 2: Heat rejected to the hot reservoir is Q₁ = Q₂ + W.
Step 3: Coefficient of performance beta is defined as desired output divided by required input: beta = Q₂ / W = Q₂ / (Q₁ - Q₂).
Step 4: Substituting Q₁ / Q₂ = T₁ / T₂, beta = T₂ / (T₁ - T₂).

graphs_and_experiments.title: P-V Diagram of Carnot Cycle
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A closed loop on a P-V plane consisting of two isothermal curves (steeper or flatter depending on coordinates, connecting (P₁,V₁) to (P₂,V₂)) and two adiabatic curves (steeper than isotherms, connecting (P₂,V₂) to (P₃,V₃) and (P₄,V₄) to (P₁,V₁)).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The area enclosed by the P-V loop represents the net mechanical work done by the Carnot engine in one complete cycle.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct questions on identifying processes (isothermal vs. adiabatic) and calculating net work or efficiency from graphical coordinates.

graphs_and_experiments.title: T-S Diagram of Carnot Cycle
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A rectangular loop on the Temperature-Entropy (T-S) plane, bounded by T = T₁, T = T₂, S = S₁, and S = S₂.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The rectangular area on the T-S diagram represents the net heat absorbed by the engine, which equals the net work done per cycle (Q_net = W = (T₁ - T₂)(S₂ - S₁)).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used to test conceptual understanding of entropy changes during isothermal (constant T, varying S) and adiabatic (constant S, isentropic) processes.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Carnot Engine Efficiency vs. Source Temperature
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A non-linear curve plotting efficiency η on the y-axis against source temperature T₁ on the x-axis, keeping sink temperature T₂ constant.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Efficiency increases non-linearly with an increase in source temperature T₁, asymptotically approaching 1 as T₁ approaches infinity.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual ranking of engine efficiencies and finding percentage changes in efficiency when source or sink temperatures are altered.

solved_numericals.question: A Carnot engine operates between reservoirs at 500 K and 300 K. If it absorbs 1200 J of heat from the source in each cycle, calculate the work done by the engine per cycle.
solution_steps: Step 1: Identify given parameters: T₁ = 500 K, T₂ = 300 K, Q₁ = 1200 J.
Step 2: Calculate efficiency using η = 1 - (T₂ / T₁).
Step 4: Use relation η = W / Q₁ to find work done: W = η * Q₁ = 0.4 * 1200 J = 480 J.

solved_numericals.question: A Carnot refrigerator absorbs heat from a freezer at -23 °C and rejects heat to the room at 27 °C. If 500 J of work is done per cycle, find the coefficient of performance and the heat rejected to the room.
solution_steps: Step 1: Convert temperatures to Kelvin: T₂ = -23 + 273 = 250 K, T₁ = 27 + 273 = 300 K.
Step 2: Calculate COP using β = T₂ / (T₁ - T₂).
Step 4: Use β = Q₂ / W to find heat absorbed: Q₂ = β * W = 5 * 500 J = 2500 J.
Step 5: Calculate heat rejected Q₁ = Q₂ + W = 2500 J + 500 J = 3000 J.

solved_numericals.question: By how much must the source temperature of a Carnot engine be increased to raise its efficiency from 40% to 50%, if the sink temperature remains constant at 300 K?
solution_steps: Step 1: Initial efficiency η₁ = 0.4, T₂ = 300 K. Using η₁ = 1 - (T₂ / T₁₁), 0.4 = 1 - (300 / T₁₁).
Step 3: Final efficiency η₂ = 0.5, T₂ = 300 K. Using η₂ = 1 - (T₂ / T₁₂), 0.5 = 1 - (300 / T₁₂).
Step 5: Change in source temperature ΔT₁ = T₁₂ - T₁₁ = 600 K - 500 K = 100 K.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumption: All processes in the Carnot cycle are strictly reversible and quasi-static, implying zero friction and infinitely slow operation.
Limitation: Reversible processes take infinite time, meaning a real Carnot engine would deliver zero practical power output.
Limitation: No real working fluid behaves as an ideal gas across extreme temperatures and pressures without intermolecular forces.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A Carnot engine can have 100% efficiency if the working substance is chosen correctly.
common_misconceptions.correct: No heat engine can have 100% efficiency unless the sink temperature T₂ = 0 K, which is thermodynamically impossible by the Third Law of Thermodynamics.
common_misconceptions.why: Efficiency is strictly governed by the temperature ratio 1 - (T₂/T₁), and T₂ can never be absolute zero.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The efficiency of a Carnot engine depends on the nature of the working gas (like monatomic vs. diatomic).
common_misconceptions.correct: The efficiency of a Carnot engine is independent of the working substance.
common_misconceptions.why: Carnot's theorem proves that efficiency depends solely on the temperatures of the source and the sink.

quick_revision: Carnot cycle consists of two isothermal and two adiabatic processes.
Efficiency depends only on absolute temperatures: η = 1 - (T₂ / T₁).
No engine can be more efficient than a reversible Carnot engine operating between the same two temperatures.
Area of P-V loop equals net work done, and area of T-S loop equals net heat absorbed.
